name: Carla Yilmaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm studying communications and marketing. A normal week is two lectures, a media production workshop, and a lot of time editing short videos in my room at Birch Court. I use AI every day, for scripts, captions, images and mock-ups of ads. I also do social media for two local cafes and a bike shop, and I get paid about 80 pounds a week from that. My dad's car dealership covers my rent and fees, so the cafe money is mine to spend or save.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you get the cafe work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I messaged them with a mock-up of what their Instagram could look like, made in an evening with AI tools. One owner, Miguel, said yes on the spot. My results at school were average, but I figured I could show what I do instead of telling people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's fine, and I'd keep using it anyway, because it already saves me hours on content. I'd tell friends who panicked that nothing is changing and they should still learn it. I'd post a funny video about the great AI panic of 2026.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means my side gig stays small but useful, and my degree stays normal. The competition would be the same as before: lots of marketing graduates and not enough decent jobs. I'd need to stand out with real client work, which I already have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the cafe clients and try to add three more this year. I'd put the work into a simple portfolio website and apply for a summer placement at an agency in the city. I'd also save about a third of what I earn, because my parents pay for everything else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and a bit bored. It's a nice, stable world, but it's not the one that makes me jump out of bed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the thing that would make you jump out of bed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting my own agency, honestly. Small, with a few clients, using AI to do what used to need five people. A plateau means that's still possible, just slower.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do your parents know about that plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mum does, and she's all for it. Dad thinks I should get a proper job first, and I'd rather do both: a placement and my own clients.

Build a portfolio **website** and apply for a summer agency placement.
Save a **third** of my side income.
feel: **Calm** and a bit bored; it's a stable world but not one that makes me jump out of bed.

fieldNote: **Adaptive** and entrepreneurial; the side work is already paying.

steps.text: Add three more small business clients this year

Save a third of my side income every month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, finally, things are getting interesting, but I'd also say that not everyone is ready. Writing, design and ads are right in the line of fire. I'd post that people who learn the tools will get ahead, and that employers should train staff instead of just cutting them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I see an opening and a threat. Entry-level marketing jobs like copywriting, scheduling and reporting will be done by software, so agencies hire fewer juniors. But small business owners will want someone who can run the tools for them, and that's what I'm already doing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd turn my side work into a proper small business with a name, invoices and a few steady clients. I'd learn the newer tools as soon as they're out, not after others. I'd also do a short course in analytics, so I'm more than a creative. And I'd try one big agency placement for the experience.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, with a flicker of worry. It's like surfing: I like waves, but I know they can knock you over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the small business clients start using the tools themselves?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd have to be better than what they can do themselves, like strategy and taste. I'd sell the thinking, not the button-pressing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you think most marketing students are doing the same?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Most of my course doesn't use the tools yet, and some are proud of it. That worries me for them, and it helps me.

steps.text: Register the side work as a small business with invoices

Apply for one big agency placement next summer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we all need to see this as the biggest change in our lifetimes and not just pretend. I'd say it would be good to talk about who owns the AI. I'd post about it, and I'd ask my parents and the cafe owners what they plan to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think marketing is exactly the kind of thinking and creative work that goes first. By 2028 an AI could do an entire campaign. My side income might vanish in the first year, because the cafes could just ask the AI themselves. That scares me more than anything about my degree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move fast. I'd start looking at what hands-on or relationship-based work I could pair with the marketing, maybe events, food or retail, where people still turn up. I'd talk to my dad about the dealership, where people still want to see and touch a car. And I'd save every pound I make, since the market could shift fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, and also wired. I'd be awake at 2am planning, then trying to sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask your dad about the dealership?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether the sales floor could use me, doing the customer side and the online side. Cars are hands-on, so they'd be safe until around 2031. It's not what I planned, but it's something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is two years enough to do anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is enough to start a different plan, not to finish it. I'd have to trade some of my degree time for building a second path.

fieldNote: The **personal** threat is to her side income, not just her degree.

steps.text: Ask Dad about working on the dealership's customer side

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is exciting and scary. I'd tell friends to build skills that mix with the tools, like taste, people skills and storytelling. And I'd say schools and employers should start now, not wait for year four.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel I'm well placed. By 2031 I'd be 23, finished with the degree, and I'd have had five years of building a client base. The risk is that the market for human marketers shrinks to nothing, but I'd have a head start and some money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd grow my client list, learn each new tool early, and look into a small business of my own. I'd save and invest a bit, probably into an index fund, and I'd keep my degree marks decent. I'd also build things I can sell that aren't just my time, like templates and short courses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful. Five years is enough time to be on the right side of this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the product you'd sell?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Simple templates for small business social media, with an AI-powered guide. Something a cafe owner can buy for 30 pounds and run themselves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if everyone does the same?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd have to be better at spotting what people actually want. The tools are the same for everyone, but taste and speed aren't.

I'd say employers should start **now**, not wait for year four.

The risk is the market for human marketers **shrinks** to nothing.

feel: **Hopeful**, because five years is enough to be on the right side.
S3.quote: The tools are the same for everyone, but taste and speed aren't.
fieldNote: Treats five years as a **head** start and builds products, not just services.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, and that it's a good moment to get ahead. I'd tell friends to try everything: tools, small projects, short jobs. I'd say it's the best time to start something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I feel quite relaxed. Ten years is my whole twenties. I'd probably have changed jobs twice and maybe started and closed a small company. A big change in 2036 would just be the setting for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, work at an agency for a year or two to learn, and start my own studio by around 22 or 23. I'd keep learning tools. I'd build savings to ride out a slow year, and I'd spend some time abroad if a chance comes up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and lucky. It feels like a long runway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the studio do in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Help small businesses tell their story in whatever form people use then. Probably a lot of AI behind the scenes, and me and two or three people in front.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could go wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could be too early, or wrong about what people want. But with ten years and a safety net from my parents, I can afford to try and fail once.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. My side income could be the first thing to vanish, and two years is not enough to build something new. What would help is basic support for people who lose work quickly, and training that's actually practical, not just a course certificate.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that my comfort comes from my parents' money, and I know that. I'd like to see ways for people without that cushion to try new things too.

headlineQuote: Most of my course doesn't use the tools yet, and some are proud of it.
portrait: Carla is an 18-year-old **marketing** student who uses AI daily and earns about 80 pounds a week from three clients.
Her father's car dealership pays her rent and fees, so her side income is her own to **save** or spend.
She is centrist and practical, sees AI as a **production** tool, and plans her own small studio.
Her mood stays calm or uneasy in most worlds, and turns **anxious** only when two years threatens her side income.
biggestWorry: The **2028** world worries her most, because her side income could vanish before she can build something new.
whatWouldHelp: Basic **support** for people who lose work quickly, plus practical training and ways for people without a cushion to try new things.
